claim: Drice is the major executioner caspase expressed in the adult brains of Drosophila.
source: We found low levels of expression of the initiator caspase Dronc in adult heads (Figure 1B). Conversely, we observed high expression of the executioner caspase Drice, whereas Dcp-1 was expressed at lower levels in adult heads (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1B shows higher expression levels of Drice compared to Dronc and Dcp-1 in adult heads.

claim: Drice is expressed in distinct regions including the mushroom bodies, subesophageal ganglions, optic lobes, and antennal lobes, with the highest levels of expression in antennal lobes.
source: We found that Drice was expressed in distinct regions, including the mushroom bodies (MBs), subesophageal ganglions (SOGs), optic lobes (OLs), and antennal lobes (ALs), which showed the highest levels of expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Histochemical analysis using streptavidin signal in Figure 1C demonstrates regional expression patterns of Drice.

claim: Drice is expressed predominantly in olfactory receptor neurons in the antennal lobe.
source: We found that Drice was expressed predominantly in ORNs in the AL (Figure 1D).
evidence: Neuron-type-specific Gal4-mediated knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1D demonstrate Drice expression in ORNs.

claim: Drice expression patterns are consistent across both males and females, indicating an absence of sex-based differences.
source: Comparisons of the expression patterns of Drice were consistent across both males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating an absence of sex-based differences, which justifies the use of males for functional simplicity in this study.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B shows comparable Drice expression patterns in male and female brains.

claim: 158 proteins were identified as highly specific to Drice::V5::TurboID flies compared to wild-type flies with a fold change greater than 10.
source: We identified 643 proteins (Figure 1G, Supplementary file 1, table S1), of which 158 were highly specific to Drice::V5::TurboID flies compared to wild-type flies (Drice::V5::TurboID/w1118>10; Figure 1G, Supplementary file 1, table S1).
evidence: LC-MS/MS analysis results shown in Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1 identify 158 Drice-proximal proteins.

claim: Drice-proximal proteins are enriched in the plasma membrane, synaptic vesicles, postsynaptic membranes, and adherens junctions.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that Drice-proximal proteins were enriched in the plasma membrane, synaptic vesicles, postsynaptic membranes, and adherens junctions (Figure 1H, Supplementary file 2, table S2).
evidence: GO analysis results in Figure 1H show enrichment of membrane-associated cellular compartments.

claim: Drice is localized primarily in cell membrane compartments rather than in the cytoplasm of the adult brain.
source: This finding suggests that Drice is localized primarily in cell membrane compartments rather than in the cytoplasm of the adult brain.
evidence: GO analysis showing enrichment of membrane proteins among Drice-proximal proteins supports this localization.

claim: The expression patterns of Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) in the adult brain closely resemble those of Drice, especially within the optic lobes, subesophageal ganglions, and antennal lobes.
source: During our analysis of proteins proximal to Drice, we discovered that the expression patterns of Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) in the adult brain closely resembled those of Drice, especially within the OLs, SOGs, and ALs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry images in Figure 2A and B show overlapping expression patterns of Drice and Fas3.

claim: Only one specific protein isoform, Fas3 isoform G (Fas3G), was identified in the LC-MS/MS analysis as a Drice-proximal protein in the adult brain.
source: Only one specific protein isoform, Fas3 isoform G (Fas3G), was identified in the LC-MS/MS analysis as a Drice-proximal protein in the adult brain (Figure 1G, Supplementary file 1, table S1).
evidence: LC-MS/MS data in Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1 identifies Fas3G as a Drice-proximal protein.

claim: Drice is predicted to interact with Fas3A (ipTM = 0.456) and Fas3G (ipTM = 0.372) rather than Fas3C (ipTM = 0.298), Fas3D/E (ipTM = 0.220), and Fas3B/F (ipTM = 0.207) using AlphaFold2-Multimer.
source: Using AlphaFold2-Multimer (Evans et al., 2021; Mirdita et al., 2022), Drice was predicted to interact with Fas3A (ipTM = 0.456) and Fas3G (ipTM = 0.372) rather than Fas3C (ipTM = 0.298), Fas3D/E (ipTM = 0.220), and Fas3B/F (ipTM = 0.207).
evidence: AlphaFold2-Multimer predictions provide computational evidence for Drice-Fas3 isoform interactions.

claim: Only Fas3G is predicted to interact with Drice with two intracellular regions among Fas3 isoforms.
source: Among Fas3 isoforms, only Fas3G is predicted to interact with Drice with two intracellular regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: PAE plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A show predicted interaction sites between Drice and Fas3G.

claim: Only Fas3G was labeled with Drice::V5::TurboID and purified using NeutrAvidin magnetic beads as detected using western blotting.
source: We confirmed that only the Fas3G was labeled with Drice::V5::TurboID and purified using NeutrAvidin magnetic beads as detected using western blotting (Figure 2F).
evidence: Western blot in Figure 2F shows specific biotinylation of Fas3G by Drice::V5::TurboID.

claim: Fas3G was highly enriched compared to other isoforms when overexpressed in ORNs in a Drice::V5::TurboID knocked-in background.
source: After proximity labeling with TurboID, followed by NeutrAvidin purification, we found that Fas3G was highly enriched compared to the other isoforms (Figure 2G).
evidence: Western blot in Figure 2G shows preferential enrichment of Fas3G after proximity labeling.

claim: Drice is proximal to a specific isoform of Fas3 in ORNs, regardless of its protein expression level.
source: These findings suggested that Drice is proximal to a specific isoform of Fas3 in ORNs, regardless of its protein expression level.
evidence: Proximity labeling experiments showing Fas3G enrichment independent of expression levels support this claim.

claim: Drice and Fas3G are proximate but do not statically interact, as Drice did not co-immunoprecipitate with Fas3G.
source: Although Fas3G was labeled by Drice::V5::TurboID, indicating its proximity to Drice within the ORNs of adult brains, Drice did not co-immunoprecipitate with Fas3G (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). This result suggests that while Drice and Fas3G are proximate, their interaction is not static, highlighting the utility of proximity labeling as a superior technique to conventional co-immunoprecipitation for identifying proteins that are spatially close.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation results in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A show no static interaction between Drice and Fas3G.

claim: None of the Fas3 isoforms are substrates for caspase.
source: However, we found that none of the Fas3 isoforms were cleaved by caspase following the induction of apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). Therefore, Fas3s are not substrates of caspase.
evidence: Western blot in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B shows no cleavage of Fas3 isoforms upon apoptosis induction.

claim: MASCaT enables highly sensitive detection of caspase activity near the plasma membrane in cells of interest reconciling with Gal4/UAS-dependent gene manipulations.
source: Therefore, our newly established reporter, MASCaT, enables the highly sensitive detection of caspase activity near the plasma membrane in cells of interest reconciling with Gal4/UAS-dependent gene manipulations.
evidence: Experimental validation of MASCaT in Drosophila S2 cells and adult brains demonstrates its functionality.

claim: MASCaT detected caspase activity specifically in the neurons of adult brains using ELAV-Gal4.
source: Using MASCaT, we detected caspase activity, specifically in the neurons of adult brains, using ELAV-Gal4 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Images in Figure 3C show MASCaT-detected caspase activity in neurons.

claim: Caspase activity was prominent in optic lobes, consistent with previously reported activation patterns detected by CaspaseTracker/CasExpress.
source: Caspase activity was prominent in OLs (Figure 3C), which is consistent with the previously reported activation pattern of caspase detected by CaspaseTracker/CasExpress (Ding et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 3C is consistent with previous reports using CaspaseTracker/CasExpress.

claim: Age-dependent caspase activation was detected in the antennal lobe and Or42b neurons.
source: Previously, we reported that a specific subset of ORNs, including Or42b neurons, undergoes age-associated caspase activation (Chihara et al., 2014). Consistent with this finding, we detected age-dependent caspase activation in the AL (Figure 3C). We further confirmed the age-dependent caspase activation in Or42b neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 3C and 3D shows age-dependent caspase activation, consistent with previous reports.

claim: Dronc induces cell loss in Or42b neurons in a catalytic-dependent manner.
source: Dronc induced cell loss while catalytically inactive Dronc (DroncCG) did not, suggesting that Dronc induces apoptosis in a catalytic-dependent manner (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Cell number quantification in Figure 4A and B shows Dronc-induced cell loss that is dependent on catalytic activity.

claim: Dcp-1 induced complete cell loss in Or42b neurons, whereas Drice did not.
source: Interestingly, although Dcp-1 induced complete cell loss, Drice did not (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that Drice requires an initiator caspase for activation, whereas Dcp-1 does not.
evidence: Cell number quantification in Figure 4A and B shows differential effects of Dcp-1 and Drice on cell survival.

claim: Drice requires an initiator caspase for activation, whereas Dcp-1 does not.
source: Interestingly, although Dcp-1 induced complete cell loss, Drice did not (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that Drice requires an initiator caspase for activation, whereas Dcp-1 does not.
evidence: Differential cell death outcomes from Drice and Dcp-1 overexpression suggest different activation requirements.

claim: Fas3G overexpression, even in combination with Drice, did not reduce the number of Or42b neurons, implying that Fas3G overexpression did not induce apoptosis.
source: However, the expression of Fas3G, even in combination with Drice, did not reduce the number of cells, implying that Fas3G overexpression did not induce apoptosis (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Cell number quantification in Figure 4C and D shows no cell loss with Fas3G overexpression.

claim: Fas3G overexpression significantly promoted caspase activation in Or42b neurons.
source: The expression of Fas3G significantly promoted caspase activation (Figure 4F and G), indicating that Fas3G regulates non-lethal caspase activation.
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 4F and G shows increased caspase activity with Fas3G overexpression.

claim: Simultaneous expression of Drice and Fas3G significantly enhanced caspase activation.
source: Moreover, the simultaneous expression of Drice and Fas3G significantly enhanced caspase activation (Figure 4F and G), signifying the promoting effect of their proximity.
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 4F and G shows synergistic enhancement of caspase activity with Drice and Fas3G co-expression.

claim: Concurrent expression of Diap-1 mitigated the caspase activation induced by Fas3G overexpression.
source: Moreover, the concurrent expression of Diap-1, an E3 ligase known to inhibit caspase activation (Ditzel et al., 2008; Hay et al., 1995; Lee et al., 2011), mitigated the caspase activation induced by Fas3G overexpression (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 4H and I shows reduced caspase activity when Diap-1 is co-expressed with Fas3G.

claim: Fas3G overexpression-facilitated non-lethal caspase activation is dependent on the core apoptotic machinery.
source: This indicates that Fas3G overexpression-facilitated non-lethal caspase activation is dependent on the core apoptotic machinery.
evidence: Diap-1-mediated suppression of Fas3G-induced caspase activation indicates dependence on apoptotic machinery.

claim: Knockdown of Fas3 or Fas3G in Or42b neurons didn't suppress the inherent, weak caspase activation.
source: Knockdown of Fas3 or Fas3G in Or42b neurons didn't suppress the inherent, weak caspase activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D shows no change in basal caspase activity with Fas3G knockdown.

claim: Drice's presence in the axon of ORNs with Fas3G was observed, yet its presence was not strictly contingent on Fas3 or Fas3G.
source: In agreement with this, Drice's presence in the axon of ORNs with Fas3G was observed, yet its presence was not strictly contingent on Fas3 or Fas3G (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E shows Drice localization independent of Fas3G.

claim: While Fas3G is not essential for mild endogenous caspase activation, overexpression of Fas3G does enhance non-lethal caspase activation in ORNs.
source: These findings collectively imply that while Fas3G is not essential for mild endogenous caspase activation, overexpression of Fas3G does enhance non-lethal caspase activation in ORNs, thus providing a valuable model for exploring the molecular processes that facilitate caspase activation without leading to cell death.
evidence: Knockdown experiments showing no effect on basal activity combined with overexpression experiments showing enhanced activity support this conclusion.

claim: Overexpression of Fas3G in ORNs markedly increased Dronc levels in those neurons.
source: We precisely analyzed the expression pattern of Dronc in adult brains and found that while its expression was low in control, overexpression of Fas3G in ORNs markedly increased Dronc levels in those neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry in Figure 5A shows increased Dronc expression with Fas3G overexpression.

claim: Dronc was found in close proximity to the overexpressed Fas3G, but not to the overexpressed Fas3C in ORNs.
source: Moreover, akin to Drice, Dronc was also found in close proximity to the overexpressed Fas3G, but not to the overexpressed Fas3C in ORNs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Western blot of proximity-labeled proteins in Figure 5B shows Dronc proximity to Fas3G but not Fas3C.

claim: Both knockdown of Dronc and the expression of the dominant-negative form of Dronc hindered the non-lethal caspase activation facilitated by Fas3G overexpression.
source: Employing MASCaT, we discovered that both knockdown of Dronc and the expression of the dominant-negative form of Dronc (DroncDN) hindered the non-lethal caspase activation facilitated by Fas3G overexpression (Figure 5C and D), indicating a dependence on initiator caspase activity.
evidence: MASCaT detection in Figure 5C and D shows reduced caspase activity when Dronc is inhibited in Fas3G-overexpressing neurons.

claim: The genetic suppression of Dronc activity did not alter the proximity between Drice and Fas3G.
source: Importantly, the genetic suppression of Dronc activity did not alter the proximity between Drice and Fas3G (Figure 5E), suggesting that the inactive Drice proform is primarily proximal to Fas3G.
evidence: Western blot of proximity-labeled proteins in Figure 5E shows maintained Drice-Fas3G proximity despite Dronc inhibition.

claim: The inactive Drice proform is primarily proximal to Fas3G.
source: Importantly, the genetic suppression of Dronc activity did not alter the proximity between Drice and Fas3G (Figure 5E), suggesting that the inactive Drice proform is primarily proximal to Fas3G.
evidence: Maintained proximity between Drice and Fas3G despite Dronc inhibition suggests the proform is proximal.

claim: Solo overexpression of Dronc led to cell death in Or42b neurons, whereas Fas3G overexpression elevated Dronc expression without causing cell death.
source: Solo overexpression of Dronc led to cell death in Or42b neurons (Figure 4A and B), whereas Fas3G overexpression elevated Dronc expression without causing cell death (Figures 4C, D, 5A).
evidence: Comparison of cell survival data from Figures 4A, B, C, D and Dronc expression data from Figure 5A shows differential outcomes.

claim: The non-lethal caspase activation driven by Fas3G overexpression is orchestrated by an increase in Dronc induced by Fas3G, bringing Dronc in close vicinity to Fas3G and thus enabling caspase activation near the plasma membrane.
source: Collectively, these findings imply that the non-lethal caspase activation driven by Fas3G overexpression is orchestrated by an increase in Dronc induced by Fas3G, bringing Dronc in close vicinity to Fas3G and thus enabling caspase activation near the plasma membrane (Figure 5F).
evidence: Integration of data showing Fas3G-induced Dronc expression, Dronc proximity to Fas3G, and Dronc-dependent caspase activation supports this mechanism.

claim: Apple cider vinegar excites six glomeruli in the antennal lobe, including DM1, which is innervated by the axons of Or42b neurons.
source: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) excites six glomeruli in the AL, including DM1, which is innervated by the axons of Or42b neurons (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: Citation to Semmelhack and Wang, 2009 provides evidence for ACV-induced glomerular activation.

claim: Or42b neurons undergo aging-dependent caspase activation and partial cell death, which reduces neuronal activity and attraction behavior in response to apple cider vinegar.
source: We have previously reported that Or42b neurons undergo aging-dependent caspase activation and partial cell death, which reduces neuronal activity and attraction behavior in response to ACV (Chihara et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Chihara et al., 2014 provides evidence for age-dependent caspase activation and behavioral effects.

claim: Inhibition of caspase activity in aged flies restores attraction behavior but does not affect that of young flies.
source: Inhibition of caspase activity in aged flies restores attraction behavior but does not affect that of young flies (Chihara et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Chihara et al., 2014 provides evidence for age-specific effects of caspase inhibition on behavior.

claim: 16 hr of starvation combined with 25% apple cider vinegar in the trap elicited a robust attraction behavior to the vinegar.
source: Using a two-choice preference assay with ACV (Figure 6A), we found that 16 hr of starvation combined with 25% ACV in the trap elicited a robust attraction behavior to the vinegar (Figure 6B).
evidence: Behavioral assay results in Figure 6B show high preference index with 16 hr starvation and 25% ACV.

claim: 4 hr of starvation with 1% apple cider vinegar in the trap resulted in milder attraction behavior, with the preference index value being close to 0 but still showing a positive trend.
source: In contrast, 4 hr of starvation with 1% ACV in the trap resulted in milder attraction behavior, with the preference index value being close to 0 but still showing a positive trend (Figure 6B).
evidence: Behavioral assay results in Figure 6B show lower preference index with 4 hr starvation and 1% ACV.

claim: Inhibition of caspase activity through expressing DroncDN didn't affect attraction behavior in young adults.
source: Under the milder experimental condition, we first confirmed that inhibition of caspase activity through expressing DroncDN didn't affect attraction behavior in young adults (Figure 6C), consistent with a previous report (Chihara et al., 2014).
evidence: Behavioral assay results in Figure 6C show no change in preference index with DroncDN expression.

claim: Overexpression of Fas3G did not impair attraction behavior and rather appeared to enhance the tendency for attraction behavior.
source: We then observed that the overexpression of Fas3G, which activates caspases, did not impair attraction behavior. Instead, it rather appeared to enhance the tendency for attraction behavior (Figure 6C), suggesting that Fas3G promotes attraction behavior.
evidence: Behavioral assay results in Figure 6C show maintained or slightly increased preference index with Fas3G overexpression.

claim: Inhibiting Fas3G overexpression-facilitated non-lethal caspase activation by expressing DroncDN strongly promoted attraction to apple cider vinegar.
source: Finally, we found that inhibiting Fas3G overexpression-facilitated non-lethal caspase activation by expressing DroncDN strongly promoted attraction to ACV (Figure 6C).
evidence: Behavioral assay results in Figure 6C show significantly increased preference index with Fas3G and DroncDN co-expression.

claim: Fas3G overexpression has a dual function: it enhances attraction behavior while also triggering non-lethal caspase activation, which counteracts the behavioral response, functioning as a regulatory brake without causing cell death.
source: Overall, these results suggest that Fas3G overexpression has a dual function: it enhances attraction behavior while also triggering non-lethal caspase activation, which counteracts the behavioral response, functioning as a regulatory brake without causing cell death.
evidence: Integration of behavioral data showing Fas3G-enhanced attraction and DroncDN-mediated further enhancement suggests opposing effects of Fas3G and caspase activation.

claim: Subcellularly restricted caspase activation mediated by caspase-proximal proteins is one of the potential mechanisms regulating caspase activation without inducing cell death.
source: Our results suggest that subcellularly restricted caspase activation mediated by caspase-proximal proteins is one of the potential mechanisms regulating caspase activation without inducing cell death.
evidence: Experimental findings showing Fas3G-mediated localized caspase activation without cell death support this mechanism.

claim: Protein proximity can be used to precisely regulate specific cellular functions by selectively cleaving a limited pool of substrates in non-lethal scenarios compared with lethal cleavages where all the substrates are potentially cleaved during apoptosis.
source: Thus, protein proximity can be used to precisely regulate specific cellular functions by selectively cleaving a limited pool of substrates in non-lethal scenarios compared with lethal cleavages where all the substrates are potentially cleaved during apoptosis.
evidence: Discussion of substrate specificity and proximity-based regulation draws on established knowledge and experimental findings.

claim: Executioner caspases, before activation as proforms, are exclusively sequestered in specific subcellular domains, including the plasma membrane of axons.
source: We showed that executioner caspases, before activation as proforms, are exclusively sequestered in specific subcellular domains, including the plasma membrane of axons.
evidence: Proximity labeling data showing enrichment of membrane proteins and localization studies support this claim.

claim: The 'hotspot' for non-lethal caspase activity appears to be determined by neighboring proteins of executioner caspases.
source: Consequently, the 'hotspot' for non-lethal caspase activity appears to be determined by these neighboring proteins of executioner caspases.
evidence: Experimental findings showing Fas3G-mediated localized caspase activation support this concept.

claim: Combining TurboID-mediated identification of proximal proteins of executioner caspases will pave the way for identifying non-lethal components and broaden our understanding of the molecular mechanism of non-lethal caspase activation.
source: Proximal proteins of executioner caspases are potential non-lethal regulators, and combining TurboID-mediated identification of these proteins will pave the way for identifying non-lethal components and broaden our understanding of the molecular mechanism of non-lethal caspase activation.
evidence: Discussion of methodological implications based on successful identification of Fas3G as a regulator.

claim: Non-lethal caspase activation antagonizes the neuronal excitability promoted by Fas3G.
source: In mice, L1CAM, an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule similar to Fas3, facilitates neuronal excitability by regulating the voltage-gated Na+ channels (Valente et al., 2016). Thus, we hypothesize that non-lethal caspase activation antagonizes the neuronal excitability promoted by Fas3G.
evidence: Hypothesis based on behavioral data and comparison to L1CAM function in mice.

claim: Non-lethal activation regulates synaptic pools and neuronal activity in a reversible manner without killing the cells.
source: In presynaptic terminals, it has been recently reported that caspase-3 modulates synaptic vesicle pools via autophagy (Gu et al., 2021). Thus, it is possible that non-lethal activation regulates synaptic pools and neuronal activity in a reversible manner without killing the cells.
evidence: Speculation based on recent findings about caspase-3 function in synaptic terminals.

claim: Suppressing neuronal activity with non-lethal reversible caspase activation is beneficial for decision-making depending on varying physiological conditions.
source: Compared with lethal activation, which irreversibly removed the neurons of interest, suppressing neuronal activity with non-lethal reversible caspase activation is beneficial for decision-making depending on their varying physiological conditions.
evidence: Discussion of functional advantages based on experimental findings and biological reasoning.

claim: Regulating caspase-proximal proteins enables non-lethal activation, which is not achieved by directly manipulating caspase expression.
source: As regulating caspase-proximal proteins enables non-lethal activation, which is not achieved by directly manipulating caspase expression, our results open the possibility of the methodological development for reversible manipulation of neuronal activity via non-lethal caspase activity.
evidence: Comparison of outcomes from Fas3G overexpression versus direct caspase overexpression supports this claim.

claim: The overexpression of Fas3G might potentially activate Dronc expression through the ecdysone signaling pathway or the Hippo signaling pathway.
source: The exact process by which Dronc expression is increased in response to Fas3G overexpression remains to be elucidated. It is known that Dronc can be upregulated via the ecdysone signaling pathway (Dorstyn et al., 1999) and the Hippo signaling pathway (Verghese et al., 2012). Therefore, the overexpression of Fas3G might potentially activate Dronc expression through one or both signaling pathways.
evidence: Speculation based on known pathways that regulate Dronc expression.

claim: Cell adhesion molecule-mediated subcellularly restricted caspase activation is conserved among species.
source: NCAM, a mammalian homologue of Fascicilin 2, is an immunoglobulin-like domain-containing cell adhesion molecule. NCAM can physically bind to caspase-8, and depending on NCAM clustering, caspase-8 and caspase-3 are activated and contribute to neurite outgrowth by cleaving its substrate spectrin (Westphal et al., 2010). Thus, it seems likely that cell adhesion molecule-mediated subcellularly restricted caspase activation is conserved among species.
evidence: Comparison to NCAM function in mammals suggests evolutionary conservation.

claim: Caspase-9/Apaf-1-dependent caspase-3 activation, without resulting in cell death, has been observed in the axon of olfactory sensory neurons during mouse development.
source: Indeed, caspase-9/Apaf-1-dependent caspase-3 activation, without resulting in cell death, has also been observed in the axon of olfactory sensory neurons during mouse development (Ohsawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation to Ohsawa et al., 2010 provides evidence for non-lethal caspase activation in mammalian olfactory neurons.

claim: The executioner caspase is pre-compartmentalized in proximity to a specific set of proteins prior to activation, poised for the initiator caspase to approach.
source: A critical insight from our research is that the executioner caspase is pre-compartmentalized in proximity to a specific set of proteins prior to activation, poised for the initiator caspase to approach.
evidence: Experimental findings showing inactive Drice proximity to Fas3G and subsequent Dronc recruitment support this model.

claim: The 'hotspot' located in the axon of the ORN may exert an inhibitory effect on neuronal activity and could also play a role in avoiding cell death by localizing caspase activity, especially during development.
source: While the 'hotspot' located in the axon of the ORN may exert an inhibitory effect on neuronal activity, it could also play a role in avoiding cell death by localizing caspase activity, especially during development.
evidence: Speculation about dual functions of localized caspase activation based on experimental findings.

claim: Tissue-preferentially expressed proteins that interact with known apoptosis regulators participate in apoptosis sensitization.
source: Recently, a protein interactome analysis in humans showed that tissue-preferentially expressed proteins that interact with known apoptosis regulators participate in apoptosis sensitization (Luck et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to Luck et al., 2020 provides evidence for tissue-specific apoptosis regulation.

claim: The identification of modulators of context-dependent apoptotic pathways will aid in understanding the precise molecular regulation of CDPs.
source: Given that CDPs are often cell- and tissue-type-specific processes, the identification of modulators of context-dependent apoptotic pathways will aid in understanding the precise molecular regulation of CDPs.
evidence: Discussion of implications based on the nature of CDPs and recent findings.

claim: Minor spliceosomes regulate alternative splicing, including Fas3, and a specific isoform of Fas3 has distinct functions and cannot be substituted by other isoforms during neuronal development.
source: A recent report showed that minor spliceosomes regulate alternative splicing, including Fas3. A specific isoform of Fas3 has distinct functions and cannot be substituted by other isoforms during neuronal development (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to Li et al., 2020 provides evidence for isoform-specific functions of Fas3.

claim: Alternative splicing may not only diversify the protein itself, but also its interaction networks to regulate module-dependent activation.
source: Our results support the idea that alternative splicing may not only diversify the protein itself, but also its interaction networks to regulate module-dependent activation.
evidence: Experimental findings showing isoform-specific proximity to Drice support this concept.
